title: Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma: From Historical Foundations to Future Therapeutic Paradigms

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Conceptual Framework of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
The earliest recognizable account of Hodgkin lymphoma is generally attributed to Thomas Hodgkin, who in 1832 described a series of patients with progressive enlargement of lymph nodes and spleen, distinguishing this clinicopathologic pattern from inflammatory and tuberculous disorders then commonly invoked to explain glandular disease ref [1]. Although Hodgkin’s original report was based on gross pathology and limited microscopy, it established the idea of a systemic lymphoid disorder with a reproducible anatomical distribution.

The disease entity was subsequently consolidated through the work of Samuel Wilks, who revisited Hodgkin’s cases and additional similar patients, formally linking the syndrome to Hodgkin’s name and helping separate it from other causes of lymphadenopathy ref [2]. Over the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, pathologists increasingly recognized that the lesion contained a characteristic minority of large atypical cells within a prominent inflammatory background, but the biological meaning of this admixture remained uncertain and the condition was variably interpreted as chronic inflammation, infection, or neoplasia.

A decisive morphological advance came with the description of the giant multinucleated cells that became eponymously associated with the disease. Sternberg’s account of localized tuberculosis-like lesions with giant cells and Reed’s later analysis of the histological picture in what she termed 'Paltauf-Sternberg’s disease' helped define the canonical Reed-Sternberg cell and anchored diagnosis in tissue morphology ref [3], ref [4]. By the mid-twentieth century, Jackson and Parker’s clinicopathologic study further systematized the histological spectrum, laying groundwork for later classifications and for the modern concept of classical Hodgkin lymphoma as a morphologically distinctive but biologically heterogeneous malignancy ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Conceptual Framework of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
Histological classification of Hodgkin lymphoma evolved from descriptive morphology to a clinicopathologic framework with biological implications. The pivotal Rye Conference formalized four categories—lymphocyte predominance, nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, and lymphocyte depletion—building on the earlier Jackson–Parker scheme and creating a common language for prognosis-oriented reporting ref [6]. This approach reflected the pre-immunophenotypic era, when classification relied largely on the abundance of reactive cells, degree of fibrosis, and the appearance of Reed–Sternberg and related cells.

Subsequent refinement came with recognition that not all entities grouped under Hodgkin disease were biologically equivalent. Lukes and Butler emphasized the importance of cellular composition and introduced concepts that helped separate paragranuloma from other forms, foreshadowing the later distinction between nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma ref [7]. The Revised European-American Lymphoma classification and, more decisively, the WHO framework integrated morphology with immunophenotype, defining classical Hodgkin lymphoma by characteristic Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells typically expressing CD30 and often CD15, while lacking the mature B-cell program seen in nodular lymphocyte-predominant cases ref [3,4].

Within classical Hodgkin lymphoma, the WHO/International Consensus approach retained the major subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted—while embedding them in a broader diagnostic algorithm that includes EBV association, distinction from grey-zone lymphomas, and recognition of overlap with primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma ref [4,5]. Thus, histological classification has shifted from a purely morphologic taxonomy toward an integrated diagnostic model linking microscopic pattern, phenotype, and disease biology.

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Conceptual Framework of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
Therapeutic progress in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is marked first by the transition from palliative irradiation to curative combined-modality strategies. Extended-field radiotherapy produced durable remissions in selected patients with localized disease, but outcomes for advanced-stage cHL remained poor. A major turning point was the introduction of combination chemotherapy with MOPP, which demonstrated that disseminated Hodgkin lymphoma could be cured with systemic treatment ref [11]. Subsequent randomized comparisons established ABVD as a less leukemogenic and ultimately more effective standard than MOPP-based programs, helping to redefine cure as an achievable goal for most patients ref [12].

A second milestone was risk-adapted treatment intensification and de-escalation. For advanced disease, the German Hodgkin Study Group showed that escalated BEACOPP improved tumor control relative to COPP/ABVD, albeit at the cost of greater acute and long-term toxicity, crystallizing the central therapeutic dilemma in cHL: maximizing cure while minimizing late effects ref [13]. In parallel, response-adapted imaging transformed management. Interim PET, particularly in the RATHL trial, enabled omission of bleomycin in PET-negative patients without compromising efficacy, exemplifying a shift from uniform treatment toward biologically informed tailoring ref [14].

More recently, targeted and immune-based therapies have expanded the therapeutic landscape. Brentuximab vedotin improved progression-free survival when incorporated into frontline therapy with AVD in the ECHELON-1 trial, while PD-1 blockade produced unprecedented activity in relapsed or refractory disease, reflecting the unique immune biology of cHL ref [15], ref [16]. These developments have moved the field beyond simple escalation toward precision balancing of efficacy, toxicity, and survivorship.

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Conceptual Framework of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
Treatment goals in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) have shifted in step with rising cure rates. Early management prioritized disease control and short-term survival, relying on extended-field radiotherapy for localized disease and later on combination chemotherapy for advanced stages. The introduction of MOPP and then ABVD reframed cHL as a curable systemic malignancy, so therapeutic success increasingly came to mean not only achieving remission but doing so with acceptable acute toxicity and reproducible long-term survival across risk groups [1,2].

As survival improved, the dominant objective moved toward preserving cure while reducing late effects. Recognition of treatment-related infertility, cardiopulmonary injury, and second malignancies led to progressive de-escalation of radiation fields and doses, risk-adapted chemotherapy, and the use of response-adapted strategies based on interim PET imaging [3,4]. In this framework, treatment goals became explicitly dual: maximize progression-free and overall survival while minimizing lifelong treatment burden for a predominantly young population.

More recently, the therapeutic aim has further evolved from uniform cure-oriented intensification to biologically and clinically individualized care. Trials incorporating brentuximab vedotin or PD-1 blockade seek to improve efficacy in high-risk or relapsed disease while potentially reducing exposure to the most toxic legacy components of therapy [5,6]. Contemporary treatment goals therefore integrate cure, survivorship, and personalization, while confronting the unresolved challenge of identifying which patients require escalation, de-escalation, or novel immune-based approaches.

subsections.section_title: Historical Evolution and Conceptual Framework of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
subsections.content:
Current conceptual challenges in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) arise from the tension between its extraordinary curability and its biological heterogeneity. cHL is defined by rare malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells embedded within a dominant, immunologically active microenvironment, making it conceptually distinct from most lymphoid malignancies and complicating efforts to identify tumor-intrinsic biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities ref [21], ref [22]. This has shifted attention from purely histologic classification toward integrated models incorporating Epstein–Barr virus status, genetic lesions affecting NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, and features of immune evasion such as 9p24.1/PD-L1–PD-L2 alterations ref [22], ref [23].

A second challenge is how to reconcile increasingly precise risk stratification with the long-standing therapeutic philosophy of maximizing cure while minimizing late toxicity. PET-adapted treatment has refined response assessment, but positive predictive value remains imperfect and de-escalation strategies raise concern about undertreatment in biologically aggressive subsets ref [24]. At the same time, the success of PD-1 blockade has reinforced the idea that cHL is an immune-dependent disease, yet optimal integration of checkpoint inhibitors across frontline, relapsed, and older-patient settings remains unsettled, particularly when balancing efficacy, fertility preservation, cardiopulmonary risk, and secondary malignancies ref [16].

Finally, cHL poses unresolved nosologic and translational questions: why morphologically similar tumors show divergent clinical behavior, how host immunity shapes both pathogenesis and treatment response, and which minimal-residual-disease or circulating biomarkers can reliably guide personalized care. These issues underscore that the modern challenge in cHL is no longer cure alone, but biologically informed cure with durable survivorship and reduced treatment burden ref [21], ref [23], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Cellular origin of Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells
subsections.content:
A central advance in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) biology was the demonstration that Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells are clonally derived from germinal-center or post-germinal-center B cells, despite their frequent loss of the canonical B-cell phenotype. Single-cell micromanipulation and immunoglobulin gene analysis showed clonal rearrangements with extensive somatic hypermutation in HRS cells, firmly linking them to antigen-experienced B cells rather than to histiocytic or other hematopoietic lineages ref [25], ref [26]. In many cases, the rearranged immunoglobulin genes carry “crippling” mutations that would prevent expression of a functional B-cell receptor, implying that precursor cells that would normally undergo apoptosis instead acquire survival signals that permit malignant outgrowth ref [27].

This paradoxical phenotype reflects profound reprogramming of lineage identity. HRS cells typically downregulate the B-cell transcriptional network, including factors required for immunoglobulin expression and maintenance of B-cell fate, while activating alternative programs associated with NF-κB signaling, activation, and cytokine production. Experimental studies identified repression of key B-cell regulators such as OCT2, BOB.1/OBF.1, and PU.1 as important contributors to the characteristic “B-cell phenotype loss” of cHL ref [28], ref [29]. These changes help explain how a tumor of B-cell origin can appear immunophenotypically discordant from its cell of origin.

The cellular origin of HRS cells therefore integrates two linked processes: derivation from germinal-center B cells that have traversed the somatic hypermutation machinery, and subsequent rescue from apoptosis through oncogenic signaling and microenvironmental support. This model provides the conceptual basis for understanding why cHL combines sparse malignant cells with extensive inflammatory dependency and why its biology is tightly coupled to mechanisms of immune evasion and niche construction ref [26], ref [27], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is defined histologically by sparse malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within a rich but non-neoplastic inflammatory background. The diagnostic tumor cells include mononuclear Hodgkin cells and multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, often accompanied by lacunar or mummified variants depending on subtype. Despite their low numerical abundance, these cells are decisive for diagnosis and are typically identified in the context of partial effacement of nodal architecture and a polymorphous infiltrate of small lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes, plasma cells, and fibroblasts ref [9], ref [22].

Histopathological classification recognizes nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted cHL, each with characteristic tissue patterns and clinical associations. Nodular sclerosis shows broad collagen bands subdividing the lymph node into nodules and frequently contains lacunar cells, whereas mixed cellularity is more diffusely infiltrative and enriched in eosinophils and histiocytes. Lymphocyte-rich cHL contains relatively numerous small B cells and fewer HRS cells, while lymphocyte-depleted cHL shows greater cytologic atypia, fewer background lymphocytes, and often extensive fibrosis or necrosis ref [9], ref [30].

Immunophenotypically, HRS cells in cHL usually express CD30 and often CD15, with weak PAX5 and frequent loss of the pan-B-cell transcriptional program; CD45 is typically absent, helping distinguish cHL from reactive mimics and many non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Modern WHO and International Consensus approaches integrate morphology, immunophenotype, and clinicopathologic context, emphasizing separation of cHL from entities such as nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, and EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell proliferations ref [10], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is architecturally defined by a striking imbalance between rare malignant Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells and an abundant, spatially organized non-malignant infiltrate. HRS cells are typically embedded within rosettes of CD4+ T cells and are surrounded by macrophages, eosinophils, mast cells, plasma cells, fibroblasts, and variable B-cell populations, creating a structured niche rather than a passive inflammatory background ref [32], ref [33]. This composition varies across histological subtypes, but in all cases the lesion behaves as a tissue ecosystem in which stromal and immune elements provide trophic support, survival signals, and physical scaffolding for tumor persistence.

The architecture of this microenvironment reflects active cellular crosstalk. HRS cells recruit and polarize neighboring leukocytes through cytokines and chemokines, while stromal remodeling promotes fibrosis, altered extracellular matrix deposition, and compartmentalization of immune cells ref [33], ref [34]. Tumor-associated macrophages are particularly prominent and have been associated with inferior outcome, consistent with an immunoregulatory and tumor-supportive role ref [35]. Fibroblasts and endothelial cells further contribute to a permissive niche by sustaining angiogenesis and facilitating leukocyte trafficking, reinforcing the chronic inflammatory morphology that is characteristic of cHL.

Recent spatial and single-cell analyses have refined this view by showing that cHL tissues contain recurrent multicellular neighborhoods enriched for HRS cells, activated/exhausted T cells, and macrophages, with immune-checkpoint ligand expression concentrated in close proximity to tumor cells ref [36]. Thus, the cHL microenvironment is best understood as a spatially organized, functionally specialized architecture that simultaneously nurtures HRS cells and constrains effective antitumor immunity.

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is sustained by a dense cytokine–chemokine circuitry in which rare Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells actively recruit and polarize abundant non-malignant cells. HRS cells secrete Th2- and Treg-attracting chemokines, particularly TARC/CCL17 and MDC/CCL22, as well as eotaxin, thereby favoring accumulation of CD4+ T cells, eosinophils, mast cells, and macrophages rather than effective cytotoxic effectors ref [37], ref [38]. This network is reinforced by reciprocal signals from stromal and immune cells, helping explain why tumor bulk in cHL is dominated by reactive infiltrates.

A central axis is constitutive activation of NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling in HRS cells, which drives expression of IL-13, IL-6, TNF-family mediators, and multiple chemokines with autocrine and paracrine functions. IL-13 is particularly notable because HRS cells both produce it and respond to it, supporting proliferation and survival, whereas IL-21/STAT3-associated programs and AP-1 activity further amplify inflammatory transcriptional outputs ref [39], ref [22]. In parallel, HRS-derived CCL5, CCL17, and CCL22, together with CXCL9 and CXCL10 in some cases, shape the spatial organization of rosetting T cells and other accessory populations around malignant cells.

These soluble networks are clinically relevant because several circulating mediators mirror disease activity. Serum TARC is elevated in many patients, correlates with tumor burden, and falls with successful therapy, making it one of the best-studied biomarkers of cHL-associated immune crosstalk ref [40]. More broadly, chemokine-driven recruitment of PD-1+ helper T cells and immunosuppressive myeloid elements integrates cytokine signaling with immune escape, underscoring that in cHL inflammation is not merely reactive but a core dependency of the malignant clone ref [38], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Immune evasion is a defining biological feature of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), in which rare Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells persist within a dense but functionally ineffective immune infiltrate. A central mechanism is genetic amplification of chromosome 9p24.1, which increases expression of the ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 and often co-amplifies JAK2, further enhancing interferon/JAK–STAT-driven checkpoint ligand expression on HRS cells ref [41]. These observations provided a mechanistic explanation for the marked susceptibility of cHL to PD-1 blockade.

The PD-1 axis in cHL is reinforced by both tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental signals. Frequent 9p24.1 alterations are accompanied by abundant PD-L1 expression on HRS cells and tumor-associated macrophages, creating a localized immunosuppressive niche that restrains effective T-cell activation ref [42], ref [35]. In Epstein–Barr virus-positive cases, latent membrane protein 1 can further augment PD-L1 expression, linking viral oncogenesis to checkpoint biology ref [43].

Immune escape in cHL also involves impaired antigen presentation. HRS cells commonly lose beta-2-microglobulin and major histocompatibility complex class I expression, and a substantial subset also shows reduced class II expression, limiting recognition by cytotoxic and helper T cells ref [44]. Consistent with this biology, PD-1 inhibitors produce unusually high response rates in relapsed/refractory cHL, validating checkpoint dependence as a disease-specific therapeutic vulnerability rather than a purely descriptive biomarker ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Genetic analyses have shown that classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is driven by a limited but recurrent set of lesions that converge on constitutive survival signaling. Copy-number gains and structural alterations affecting REL, JAK2, and the 9p24.1 locus are frequent, while mutations in negative regulators such as TNFAIP3/A20 and SOCS1 further amplify NF-κB and JAK/STAT activity in Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells ref [45], ref [46]. These lesions help explain how a sparse malignant clone can remain viable despite extensive loss of the normal B-cell transcriptional program.

Sequencing studies also indicate marked interpatient heterogeneity, but recurrently altered pathways are biologically coherent. Mutations in B2M, CD58, XPO1, GNA13, ITPKB, and components of antigen-presentation and cytokine-signaling machinery support immune escape, aberrant trafficking, and sustained proliferation ref [47], ref [48]. Integrative genomic work has therefore emphasized pathway-level convergence rather than a single dominant driver, with frequent cooperation between copy-number change, somatic mutation, and microenvironmental selection.

Epigenetically, cHL is characterized by extensive reprogramming that suppresses the mature B-cell phenotype and stabilizes an inflammatory, immune-evasive state. Promoter methylation and chromatin remodeling contribute to silencing of B-cell lineage regulators, while altered activity of epigenetic modifiers such as EZH2, CREBBP/EP300-associated networks, and HDAC-dependent programs reinforces the Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg transcriptional identity ref [49], ref [50]. These findings provide a rationale for therapeutic strategies that combine pathway inhibition with epigenetic modulation.

subsections.section_title: Pathobiology, Tumor Microenvironment, and Molecular Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is implicated in a substantial subset of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), with prevalence varying by age, geography, histologic subtype, and immune status. EBV-positive cHL is particularly enriched in mixed-cellularity disease, in childhood and older-age cases, and in immunosuppressed populations, supporting an etiologic contribution in at least a subset of tumors rather than a merely incidental association ref [51], ref [52]. Detection of clonal EBV genomes within Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells further indicates that viral infection precedes or accompanies malignant outgrowth ref [53].

At the cellular level, EBV-positive cHL typically displays a restricted latency II program, characterized by expression of EBNA1, LMP1, and LMP2A. These latent proteins can substitute for key survival signals normally required in germinal-center B cells: LMP1 functionally mimics CD40 signaling, whereas LMP2A can provide B-cell receptor-like tonic input, thereby helping rescue crippled immunoglobulin-deficient precursors from apoptosis ref [54], ref [55]. Through activation of NF-kB, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT-linked pathways, EBV complements host genetic lesions that promote HRS-cell survival and cytokine production.

EBV also shapes the immune microenvironment. Viral antigenicity is counterbalanced by strong local immunoregulatory circuits, including abundant PD-L1 expression on HRS cells and surrounding myeloid elements, which may be further enhanced in EBV-positive cases and contribute to ineffective antiviral antitumor immunity ref [56]. Thus, EBV in cHL is best viewed as a context-dependent oncogenic cofactor that intersects with B-cell reprogramming, inflammatory signaling, and immune escape.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is an uncommon but globally distributed malignancy whose incidence varies substantially by geography, age structure, and socioeconomic context. Population-based analyses consistently show that Hodgkin lymphoma has one of the most distinctive age-incidence profiles in oncology, with a prominent peak in adolescents and young adults and, in many high-income settings, a second peak in later life ref [57], ref [58]. By contrast, in lower-income regions the disease more often presents in childhood or early adulthood, reflecting differences in population age distribution, exposure patterns, and subtype composition ref [58], ref [59].

Demographic heterogeneity also reflects the biologic diversity of cHL. The nodular sclerosis subtype predominates in adolescents and young adults in industrialized countries, whereas mixed cellularity disease is relatively more frequent in children, older adults, and populations from low- and middle-income settings; these patterns parallel variation in Epstein–Barr virus association and host immune environment ref [59], ref [60]. A modest male predominance is observed overall, although sex ratios vary by age and histologic subtype ref [57], ref [60].

Temporal trends suggest that age-standardized incidence has been relatively stable or only slowly changing in many regions, while survival has improved markedly because of advances in staging, supportive care, and combined-modality therapy ref [57], ref [61]. Nonetheless, global burden remains uneven, with poorer outcomes in resource-constrained settings where delayed diagnosis, limited pathology infrastructure, and treatment access continue to shape epidemiologic patterns ref [61], ref [62].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
The etiology of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is multifactorial, reflecting interactions among host immune status, infectious exposures, and genetic susceptibility. Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is the most consistently implicated infectious cofactor, although its contribution varies by age, geography, histologic subtype, and immunologic context. Molecular studies demonstrating clonal EBV genomes in Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells support a direct pathogenetic role in a subset of tumors, particularly mixed cellularity cHL and cases arising in children, older adults, and immunocompromised patients ref [63].

Immune dysregulation is a major predisposing condition. The risk of Hodgkin lymphoma is markedly elevated in people living with HIV and was already evident in large registry-linkage analyses before the modern antiretroviral era ref [64]. A related signal is seen after iatrogenic immunosuppression, including solid-organ transplantation, where impaired T-cell surveillance and EBV-driven lymphoproliferation increase lymphoma risk ref [65]. Familial aggregation and twin studies further indicate inherited susceptibility, consistent with polygenic effects in HLA and non-HLA immune-response loci ref [66].

Several epidemiologic observations also point to early-life and environmental determinants. Delayed exposure to common childhood infections, smaller sibship size, and higher socioeconomic setting have been linked to the young-adult cHL peak, forming the basis of the long-standing "late infection" hypothesis ref [67]. More recently, pooled analyses have identified obesity as a modest but reproducible risk factor for Hodgkin lymphoma, suggesting that chronic inflammatory and metabolic perturbations may contribute to disease predisposition ref [68].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) often presents with painless peripheral lymphadenopathy, most commonly in the cervical or supraclavicular regions, although mediastinal involvement is frequent and may dominate the presentation in nodular sclerosis disease. Extranodal disease is less common at diagnosis than in many aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphomas, but contiguous spread to adjacent nodal groups and mediastinal bulk are characteristic patterns reflected in modern clinical descriptions of cHL ref [69], ref [70].

Systemic symptoms remain central to the clinical phenotype and to initial risk assessment. The classic “B symptoms”—unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss—identify a subgroup with greater inflammatory burden and are incorporated into staging conventions. Pruritus, fatigue, alcohol-induced pain, and cough or dyspnea from mediastinal masses can substantially affect quality of life even before treatment, while splenic or hepatic involvement may produce abdominal discomfort or early satiety in advanced disease ref [70], ref [71].

Symptom burden in cHL is shaped not only by tumor bulk but also by host inflammatory signaling. Elevated circulating cytokines and acute-phase reactants correlate with constitutional symptoms, anemia, and reduced performance status, reinforcing the link between the biologic microenvironment and clinical presentation. In contemporary practice, careful baseline documentation of constitutional symptoms, compressive manifestations, and patient-reported functional impairment is important because these features inform staging, urgency of imaging and biopsy, and subsequent response assessment ref [72], ref [73].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
Diagnosis of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) rests on excisional or core tissue biopsy showing scattered Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells within a characteristic inflammatory milieu; fine-needle aspiration alone is generally insufficient because architectural context is critical for distinguishing cHL from reactive conditions and other lymphomas. The current WHO/International Consensus framework recognizes the major histologic subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted—while emphasizing correlation of morphology with immunophenotype and clinical setting to avoid confusion with nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma and mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma ref [9], ref [74].

Immunophenotypically, HRS cells in cHL typically express CD30 strongly and CD15 in most cases, show weak Pax5 reflecting crippled B-cell lineage, and are usually negative or only variably positive for pan-leukocyte and B-cell markers such as CD45 and CD20; EBER in situ hybridization is useful for identifying Epstein–Barr virus-associated cases, particularly in mixed cellularity and immunodeficiency-related disease ref [74], ref [75]. Broad panels are often required because a minority of cases are CD15-negative or show aberrant marker expression, and ancillary stains help separate cHL from anaplastic large cell lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and gray zone lymphoma ref [76].

Beyond routine diagnosis, pathology contributes to baseline risk assessment by documenting subtype, extent of necrosis or fibrosis, and EBV status, while emerging studies indicate that the composition of the tumor microenvironment has prognostic relevance. In particular, gene-expression and immunohistochemical analyses have linked macrophage-rich microenvironments with inferior outcomes, highlighting how cHL diagnosis increasingly integrates neoplastic-cell phenotype with stromal and immune contexture ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
Staging in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) remains anchored in the Ann Arbor framework, subsequently refined at the Cotswolds meeting to improve the definition of nodal regions, bulky disease, and extranodal involvement and to standardize notation for constitutional symptoms and tumor bulk ref [77], ref [78]. In routine practice, stage assignment still distinguishes limited from advanced disease, but contemporary disease assessment integrates anatomic extent with mediastinal bulk, contiguous versus disseminated extranodal disease, performance status, and laboratory parameters that influence therapeutic intensity.

The major conceptual shift in staging has been the incorporation of fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT into baseline assessment. International recommendations emphasize PET/CT as the preferred modality for initial staging because it more accurately detects nodal and extranodal sites than conventional CT and can alter stage in a clinically meaningful proportion of patients ref [79], ref [80]. PET-based assessment has also reduced the role of routine bone marrow biopsy, which is now often omitted when PET/CT shows no marrow involvement, given its high negative predictive value in cHL ref [80], ref [81].

For response-adapted management, disease assessment increasingly relies on standardized metabolic criteria. The Lugano classification and subsequent international harmonization efforts endorse the Deauville 5-point scale for interim and end-of-treatment PET interpretation, linking baseline staging to dynamic assessment of chemosensitivity and residual disease burden ref [80], ref [82]. Thus, modern staging in cHL is best viewed not as a static anatomic exercise, but as the first step in an integrated risk-assessment pathway combining extent of disease, bulk, symptoms, and early metabolic response.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.content:
Imaging is central to the diagnosis, staging, and response assessment of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). Contrast-enhanced CT remains important for defining nodal and extranodal anatomy, but fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography combined with CT (FDG-PET/CT) has become the reference functional modality because cHL is typically highly FDG-avid. International recommendations incorporated PET/CT into routine initial staging and treatment evaluation, enabling more accurate delineation of disease extent than CT alone and providing a metabolic baseline for subsequent comparison ref [80], ref [83].

PET-based response assessment is now standardized through the Deauville 5-point scale, which improved interobserver consistency and underpins modern response-adapted strategies in both early and advanced disease ref [83], ref [84]. The prognostic value of interim PET, particularly after two cycles of ABVD, was established in prospective studies showing strong associations between early metabolic response and progression-free survival, thereby supporting escalation or de-escalation approaches in selected patients ref [85], ref [14]. End-of-treatment PET/CT is also preferred for confirming remission and distinguishing residual scar tissue from viable lymphoma ref [80], ref [84].

Although PET/CT is dominant, modality selection should still reflect clinical context. CT is widely available and remains useful when PET is inaccessible or for urgent assessment of bulky mediastinal disease, while PET/CT may produce false-positive uptake from infection, inflammation, thymic rebound, or treatment-related effects. Emerging interest in whole-body MRI and diffusion-weighted imaging reflects a desire to reduce radiation exposure, especially in children, adolescents, and young adults, but these techniques are not yet universal replacements for PET/CT in routine cHL staging ref [86].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnostic Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Prognostic indices and baseline risk stratification
subsections.content:
Baseline risk stratification in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is anchored in clinical stage, bulk, systemic symptoms, extranodal involvement, and selected laboratory variables, with the practical goal of separating patients into favorable, intermediate, and advanced-risk groups for treatment selection. In advanced-stage disease, the International Prognostic Score (IPS) remains the canonical pretreatment index, originally incorporating seven adverse factors including age, stage IV disease, anemia, leukocytosis, lymphocytopenia, male sex, and hypoalbuminemia; although outcomes have improved in the modern era, IPS still captures a gradient of baseline risk, particularly at higher scores ref [87], ref [88].

For limited-stage cHL, baseline stratification is usually trial-group specific rather than universally standardized. The European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC), German Hodgkin Study Group (GHSG), and National Comprehensive Cancer Network use overlapping adverse features such as large mediastinal mass, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, multiple nodal areas, B symptoms, and extranodal disease to define early favorable versus early unfavorable presentations, thereby guiding the intensity of combined-modality or chemotherapy-alone approaches ref [89], ref [90].

Contemporary practice increasingly integrates biologic and imaging-based markers with these clinical scores. Reassessment of IPS in the PET era has shown attenuation of some individual variables, yet baseline risk remains relevant when interpreted alongside metabolic tumor burden and subsequent response-adapted imaging. More recently, circulating tumor DNA has emerged as a promising complementary baseline biomarker associated with tumor burden and treatment outcome, although it is not yet part of routine frontline risk models ref [88], ref [91], ref [92].

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
The central principle of first-line therapy in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is to preserve its very high curability while limiting acute toxicity and late effects. This balance has historically been shaped by the replacement of extended-field radiotherapy alone with multi-agent chemotherapy and combined-modality strategies, most notably ABVD, which achieved durable disease control with less infertility and secondary leukemia than older MOPP-based programs ref [93], ref [94]. In contemporary practice, treatment intensity is selected according to stage, bulk, B symptoms, and other adverse features, with the expectation that most patients can be cured with planned frontline therapy.

Another core principle is that regimen choice must reflect the trade-off between efficacy and treatment-related harm. Escalated BEACOPP improves tumor control in high-risk advanced disease but at the cost of substantially greater hematologic, infectious, gonadal, and secondary malignancy risks, making it appropriate only for selected patients and settings ref [13]. Conversely, incorporation of brentuximab vedotin into AVD has provided an alternative intensification strategy that improves modified progression-free survival relative to ABVD while avoiding bleomycin exposure, albeit with more neuropathy and neutropenia ref [15].

Accordingly, modern first-line management is increasingly risk-adapted and response-adapted rather than uniform. Baseline prognostic models, such as the International Prognostic Score for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, help estimate pretreatment risk, whereas interim FDG-PET allows early assessment of chemosensitivity and supports de-escalation or escalation strategies in subsequent cycles ref [87], ref [95]. These principles underpin current stage-specific treatment algorithms discussed in the following subsections.

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.subsection_title: Management of early-stage favorable and unfavorable disease
subsections.content:
Management of early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is anchored in cure preservation while limiting late toxicity, especially second cancers and cardiovascular disease. Contemporary practice separates favorable from unfavorable disease using cooperative-group risk factors such as bulky mediastinal disease, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, multiple nodal sites, B symptoms, or extranodal involvement, because these features predict relapse risk and influence the intensity of combined-modality therapy. In favorable disease, abbreviated doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD) followed by limited-field radiotherapy has long been a standard, based on randomized evidence showing that two cycles of ABVD plus 20 Gy involved-field radiotherapy can maintain excellent tumor control in selected patients ref [18].

For early-stage unfavorable cHL, treatment has generally been intensified relative to favorable presentations, most commonly with four cycles of ABVD plus consolidative radiotherapy, although some European programs have used more intensive regimens such as escalated BEACOPP-based approaches in selected patients. The GHSG HD11 trial established that combined-modality therapy remained effective in unfavorable early-stage disease and informed dose and regimen selection ref [96]. Subsequent PET-adapted studies sought to reduce radiotherapy exposure in patients achieving early metabolic remission, but omission of radiotherapy after chemotherapy alone has usually produced a small increase in relapse risk despite high overall survival, as shown in RAPID and EORTC/LYSA/FIL H10 ref [97], ref [98].

Accordingly, current management of early-stage disease balances disease control against survivorship concerns: combined-modality therapy remains the benchmark for most favorable and unfavorable patients, whereas chemotherapy-alone strategies are generally reserved for carefully selected PET-negative patients willing to accept a modestly higher risk of recurrence. More recently, the GHSG HD17 trial suggested that in PET-negative early unfavorable disease, radiotherapy may be omitted after intensified combined chemotherapy without compromising progression-free survival, supporting increasingly individualized, risk-adapted care ref [99].

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
Advanced-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) has historically been treated with full-course multiagent chemotherapy, with ABVD becoming the benchmark because it preserves high cure rates while limiting infertility and late leukemogenesis relative to escalated alkylator-intensive programs. Nevertheless, a persistent tension in stage III–IV disease is the trade-off between maximizing initial disease control and minimizing acute pulmonary, hematologic, and long-term toxicities. This tension drove comparative trials of ABVD against more intensive BEACOPP strategies, which improved tumor control in selected high-risk populations but at the cost of substantially greater treatment burden ref [100], ref [101].

Contemporary management therefore emphasizes risk-adapted intensification or de-escalation rather than uniform treatment escalation. PET-guided strategies have been central: the RATHL trial showed that patients with a negative interim PET after ABVD could safely omit bleomycin and continue with AVD, reducing pulmonary toxicity without compromising outcomes, whereas PET-positive patients were candidates for treatment intensification ref [14]. In parallel, incorporation of brentuximab vedotin into frontline therapy provided a non-bleomycin alternative; the ECHELON-1 trial demonstrated improved modified progression-free survival for A+AVD versus ABVD in advanced-stage disease, although with more neuropathy and neutropenia ref [15].

Current treatment selection in advanced-stage cHL thus integrates stage, International Prognostic Score–defined risk, age, comorbidity, and toxicity priorities. Escalated BEACOPP remains relevant for some very high-risk or PET-positive patients, but many centers favor PET-adapted ABVD/AVD-based approaches or brentuximab-containing regimens to preserve cure while reducing late effects ref [14], ref [15], ref [102]. Ongoing refinement focuses on identifying which patients truly benefit from upfront intensification and which can be cured with less toxic therapy ref [102], ref [103].

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
Interim fluorodeoxyglucose PET, typically performed after two cycles of chemotherapy (PET2), has become a central tool for response-adapted management in classical Hodgkin lymphoma because it provides an early in vivo measure of chemosensitivity. Standardization through the Deauville 5-point scale enabled reproducible interpretation and integration into clinical trials, allowing treatment intensification for inadequate early responders and de-escalation for patients with rapid metabolic remission ref [80].

In early-stage disease, PET-adapted strategies have mainly tested whether radiotherapy can be omitted in PET-negative patients to reduce late toxicity. Trials such as RAPID and the EORTC/LYSA/FIL H10 study showed that omission of consolidative radiotherapy after a negative interim PET modestly increases relapse risk, even though overall survival remains high because of effective salvage therapy ref [104], ref [85]. These findings established interim PET as a powerful risk-stratification tool, while also underscoring that the clinical value of de-escalation depends on balancing relapse prevention against long-term treatment sequelae.

In advanced-stage cHL, interim PET has been used both to escalate therapy from ABVD in PET-positive patients and to de-escalate bleomycin exposure in PET-negative patients. The RATHL trial demonstrated that patients with negative PET2 could safely omit bleomycin and continue AVD, reducing pulmonary toxicity without compromising outcomes, whereas PET-positive patients benefited from treatment intensification ref [14]. More intensive PET-adapted approaches, including escalation based on early PET after BEACOPP-based therapy, were also supported by the HD18 trial ref [105]. Collectively, these studies established interim PET as a practical framework for risk-adapted therapy, although its interpretation must remain context-specific and integrated with baseline risk, regimen, and goals of survivorship.

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
Radiotherapy remains an important component of curative therapy in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), but its role has narrowed substantially in the modern era. Historical use of extended-field irradiation has been replaced by involved-site or involved-node radiotherapy, reflecting improved imaging, more effective systemic therapy, and a stronger emphasis on limiting late toxicity. Contemporary planning therefore prioritizes reduction of dose to the heart, lungs, breast, thyroid, and other organs at risk while maintaining local control, particularly in early-stage disease and in selected patients with residual PET-positive sites after chemotherapy ref [106], ref [107].

Randomized PET-adapted studies have helped define when radiotherapy can be omitted. In the RAPID trial, patients with stage IA/IIA non-bulky disease who were PET-negative after three cycles of ABVD had very favorable outcomes overall, although omission of consolidative radiotherapy was associated with a modest increase in relapse risk ref [108]. Similarly, the EORTC/LYSA/FIL H10 trial showed that abandoning radiotherapy in early PET-negative patients led to more early recurrences, reinforcing that radiotherapy remains the most reliable means of maximizing disease control in many early-stage presentations ref [109].

Modern delivery techniques seek to preserve this benefit with less harm. ILROG guidance has standardized smaller target volumes and advanced planning approaches, including deep-inspiration breath hold, IMRT, and proton therapy in selected mediastinal cases, to reduce integral dose and long-term cardiopulmonary and second-cancer risks ref [107]. The rationale for this de-escalation is supported by large survivorship analyses showing substantial excess late mortality from cardiovascular disease and subsequent malignancy after older radiation-intensive approaches ref [110], ref [111].

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
Because contemporary frontline therapy cures most patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, toxicity has become a central determinant of regimen selection and treatment intensity. Acute toxicities are dominated by myelosuppression, infection risk, neuropathy, mucositis, nausea, and bleomycin-associated pulmonary injury, the latter being particularly relevant in ABVD-based approaches and in older adults. In contrast, escalated BEACOPP improves disease control in selected advanced-stage populations at the cost of substantially greater hematologic toxicity, infertility risk, and treatment-related morbidity, reinforcing the rationale for risk-adapted de-escalation when possible ref [13], ref [112].

Long-term survivorship concerns are equally important. Alkylator exposure and pelvic irradiation are strongly linked to gonadal dysfunction and infertility, while anthracyclines and mediastinal radiotherapy contribute to late cardiovascular disease. In addition, historical extended-field radiotherapy and combined-modality treatment have been associated with excess second malignant neoplasms, including breast, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers, with risks that may persist for decades after cure ref [113], ref [110]. These observations have driven modern efforts to limit cumulative chemotherapy exposure, reduce radiation fields and dose, and omit radiotherapy in carefully selected PET-responsive patients.

Accordingly, toxicity mitigation is now embedded in frontline management: baseline assessment of pulmonary, cardiac, and fertility risks; age- and comorbidity-sensitive regimen choice; avoidance of unnecessary bleomycin or radiotherapy; and structured long-term surveillance for cardiovascular disease and second cancers. The survivorship burden documented in long-term cohort studies underpins the shift from maximally intensive therapy toward strategies that preserve cure while minimizing late effects ref [110], ref [114].

subsections.section_title: Conventional Therapeutic Approaches and Risk-Adapted Management
subsections.content:
Frontline management of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) requires modification in special populations in whom standard curative therapy may confer disproportionate toxicity. In older adults, outcomes are limited not only by adverse biology and comorbidity, but also by treatment intolerance, particularly bleomycin-associated pulmonary injury. Population- and trial-based analyses have consistently shown inferior survival and greater treatment-related mortality in this group, supporting attenuation of bleomycin exposure, careful geriatric assessment, and selection of anthracycline-based but less toxic platforms when feasible ref [115], ref [116].

Pregnancy presents a distinct scenario in which maternal cure and fetal safety must be balanced. Contemporary reviews and guideline-oriented analyses support deferring therapy until postpartum for asymptomatic or limited disease when possible, while using selected chemotherapy after the first trimester for symptomatic or progressive cHL; radiotherapy is generally avoided during pregnancy except in highly selected circumstances ref [117]. Fertility preservation is another frontline consideration, especially for adolescents and young adults. Although ABVD is relatively less gonadotoxic than escalated BEACOPP, pretreatment counseling regarding sperm cryopreservation, oocyte/embryo preservation, and anticipated reproductive risk should be incorporated into initial management planning ref [118].

Patients with HIV-associated cHL can achieve outcomes approaching those of the general population when treated with curative-intent regimens alongside effective antiretroviral therapy and antimicrobial prophylaxis. Prospective multicenter data with ABVD in the combined antiretroviral era support standard-dose treatment in appropriately supported patients, emphasizing that HIV status alone should not preclude guideline-concordant frontline therapy ref [119].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
For patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma who remain candidates for autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), salvage chemotherapy has traditionally served two purposes: cytoreduction and identification of chemosensitive disease. Common platinum- or gemcitabine-based regimens, including ICE, DHAP/ESHAP, GVD, and IGEV, can induce substantial response rates, but complete metabolic remission before ASCT has emerged as a more important prognostic benchmark than conventional anatomic response alone ref [120], ref [121].

The incorporation of functional imaging has therefore reshaped response assessment. Fluorodeoxyglucose PET performed after salvage therapy is strongly associated with post-transplant progression-free survival, and PET negativity before ASCT consistently identifies a group with superior outcomes compared with patients who remain PET positive ref [122], ref [123]. These observations have supported PET-adapted decision making, including escalation or alteration of salvage therapy in patients with inadequate metabolic response rather than proceeding directly to transplant.

More recent studies have sought to improve pre-ASCT PET negativity by integrating novel agents into salvage programs. Brentuximab vedotin used sequentially or in combination with chemotherapy has increased complete response rates while preserving stem-cell mobilization feasibility, offering an alternative to conventional multi-agent cytotoxic salvage alone ref [124], ref [125]. In current practice, salvage selection is therefore individualized according to disease tempo, prior treatment exposure, comorbidity, and the need to maximize metabolic remission before ASCT.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) remains the historical standard of care for fit patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma whose disease demonstrates chemosensitivity to salvage therapy. Early randomized and comparative studies established a progression-free survival advantage for high-dose therapy followed by ASCT over conventional-dose salvage approaches, thereby defining transplantation as the preferred consolidative strategy in first relapse for eligible patients ref [126], ref [127]. In contemporary practice, ASCT is generally pursued after second-line treatment once adequate disease control and stem-cell mobilization are achieved.

Pre-transplant disease status is one of the strongest determinants of outcome. Functional imaging has refined risk stratification, and patients who enter ASCT with positron emission tomography (PET)-negative disease have substantially superior progression-free survival compared with those with persistent PET-avid lymphoma, supporting PET-adapted salvage strategies and, in some centers, additional therapy before proceeding to transplantation ref [128], ref [129]. Nonetheless, ASCT can still provide durable remission for a subset of patients with residual metabolic activity, particularly when followed by effective post-transplant consolidation.

Current outcomes after ASCT are shaped not only by disease chemosensitivity but also by relapse timing, extranodal involvement, B symptoms, and prior treatment burden. Long-term series confirm that cure remains achievable for many patients, although relapse after ASCT identifies a population with biologically higher-risk disease that increasingly requires integration of brentuximab vedotin, PD-1 blockade, or cellular strategies ref [130], ref [131]. Thus, ASCT continues to occupy a central but evolving role within a broader, response-adapted therapeutic sequence.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Post-transplant consolidation aims to reduce relapse after autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), particularly in patients with adverse features such as primary refractory disease, early relapse, extranodal involvement, or PET-positive salvage responses. The strongest randomized evidence supports brentuximab vedotin maintenance: in the phase III AETHERA trial, post-ASCT brentuximab vedotin significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in high-risk classical Hodgkin lymphoma, establishing a standard option for selected patients ref [132]. Longer-term follow-up confirmed durable disease-control benefit, although the absence of a clear overall survival advantage and the risk of cumulative peripheral neuropathy have informed more individualized use ref [133].

In contemporary practice, the role of brentuximab vedotin maintenance is shaped by prior exposure during salvage therapy and by depth of response before transplant. Real-world studies suggest that benefit may persist in high-risk patients, but toxicity, prior brentuximab resistance, and evolving checkpoint inhibitor–based salvage strategies complicate routine application ref [134]. Accordingly, many centers reserve consolidation for patients with persistent biologic or imaging-defined risk after ASCT rather than applying it uniformly.

Checkpoint inhibitor maintenance remains investigational but biologically attractive. Early phase studies of pembrolizumab after ASCT have shown feasible administration and encouraging progression-free survival in very high-risk populations, supporting ongoing efforts to integrate immune-based consolidation into post-transplant care ref [135]. Similar signal-seeking work with nivolumab has also suggested activity in the post-ASCT setting ref [136]. Current decision-making therefore balances established evidence for brentuximab vedotin against prior treatment history, neuropathy risk, and the prospect that immunologic consolidation may further refine relapse prevention.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Brentuximab vedotin (BV), an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate delivering monomethyl auristatin E, transformed the management of relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) by exploiting the near-universal expression of CD30 on Reed-Sternberg cells. In the pivotal phase II study after autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) failure, BV produced high overall and complete response rates with a subset of durable remissions, establishing single-agent activity in heavily pretreated disease ref [137]. Five-year follow-up confirmed that a minority of patients achieved prolonged disease control without further therapy, supporting the possibility of functional cure in selected responders ref [138].

BV also moved earlier in the treatment algorithm as consolidation after ASCT for patients with high-risk features. The randomized AETHERA trial demonstrated improved progression-free survival with post-transplant BV maintenance versus placebo, although peripheral neuropathy emerged as the principal cumulative toxicity ref [139]. In the pre-transplant setting, BV has been incorporated into salvage strategies either sequentially or in combination with chemotherapy to increase PET-negative remission rates before ASCT, reflecting its favorable activity-to-tolerability profile compared with traditional multi-agent cytotoxic regimens ref [140].

Beyond monotherapy, CD30-targeted treatment has evolved through rational combinations and next-generation constructs. BV plus nivolumab has shown high complete metabolic response rates as a chemotherapy-sparing salvage approach before ASCT, illustrating the complementary biology of CD30 targeting and checkpoint blockade ref [141]. Nevertheless, resistance, neuropathy, and diminished efficacy after prior exposure remain practical limitations, motivating ongoing evaluation of alternative anti-CD30 platforms and optimized sequencing in multiply relapsed disease.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed the management of relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), a disease uniquely enriched for 9p24.1 amplification and consequent PD-L1/PD-L2 overexpression on Reed–Sternberg cells and the surrounding microenvironment. This biologic dependence provided a compelling rationale for PD-1 blockade, and early-phase studies with nivolumab and pembrolizumab demonstrated high response rates and durable disease control in heavily pretreated patients, including many who had progressed after autologous transplantation and brentuximab vedotin ref [16], ref [142].

Subsequent multicenter experience confirmed that PD-1 inhibitors can induce prolonged remissions with a favorable toxicity profile relative to conventional cytotoxic salvage, although complete response rates remain lower than overall response rates and late relapses still occur. Pembrolizumab also showed superiority over brentuximab vedotin in the randomized phase III KEYNOTE-204 trial, supporting its use as a preferred option in many patients with relapsed disease not immediately proceeding to transplantation ref [143]. In parallel, response-adapted incorporation of nivolumab with chemotherapy in the salvage setting has produced high metabolic complete response rates before autologous transplantation, suggesting an important bridge-to-transplant role ref [144].

Current challenges concern optimal sequencing, treatment duration, and management after PD-1 failure. Primary and acquired resistance likely reflect multifactorial immune escape beyond PD-1 dependence, prompting evaluation of combinations with chemotherapy, brentuximab vedotin, CTLA-4 blockade, and cellular therapies. For selected patients, checkpoint inhibition may defer transplantation or improve pretransplant disease control, but decisions must be individualized because prior PD-1 exposure can influence subsequent allogeneic transplantation toxicity, particularly graft-versus-host disease and other immune complications ref [145].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) now occupies a narrower but still important role in relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma, chiefly for patients with disease progressing after autologous transplantation, brentuximab vedotin, and/or PD-1 blockade. Reduced-intensity conditioning expanded access and demonstrated durable disease control consistent with a graft-versus-lymphoma effect, while lowering non-relapse mortality relative to historical myeloablative approaches ref [146], ref [147]. Contemporary selection therefore emphasizes chemosensitive or at least controllable disease, performance status, donor availability, and prior exposure to immunotherapy.

Checkpoint inhibitor exposure has altered the allo-HCT risk-benefit calculus. Although remissions induced by nivolumab or pembrolizumab can facilitate bridging to transplant, several series reported increased early immune toxicity, including severe acute graft-versus-host disease and noninfectious febrile syndromes, particularly with short washout intervals ref [148], ref [149]. These observations have prompted careful timing, intensified GVHD prophylaxis in some centers, and individualized donor/platform choices rather than routine transplantation for all patients responding to PD-1 blockade.

Cellular immunotherapy beyond allo-HCT remains investigational. CD30-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy has shown feasibility and meaningful activity in heavily pretreated Hodgkin lymphoma, with manageable cytokine release syndrome and occasional durable remissions, but response durability and optimal integration with prior or subsequent PD-1 blockade remain unsettled ref [150], ref [151]. Thus, for multiply relapsed or biologically high-risk disease, allo-HCT and emerging cellular approaches are best viewed as complementary options within a sequential strategy guided by response depth, prior immune exposure, and transplant-related risk.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Advances in Relapsed, Refractory, and High-Risk Disease
subsections.content:
Therapeutic sequencing in relapsed/refractory cHL is increasingly shaped by the relative efficacy and toxicity of brentuximab vedotin (BV), PD-1 blockade, and transplantation. Contemporary data suggest that PD-1 inhibitors produce high response rates even after BV exposure and can induce meaningful remissions that permit subsequent autologous transplantation, supporting their use either before or after BV depending on prior treatment history, tempo of relapse, and transplant eligibility [1,2]. Conversely, BV retains activity after prior chemotherapy and remains relevant for patients needing rapid cytoreduction or combination salvage approaches, although durability is limited in multiply pretreated disease [3].

Resistance patterns are biologically distinct across these classes. BV resistance may reflect heterogeneous CD30 expression, impaired intracellular payload delivery, and multidrug resistance mechanisms, whereas PD-1 resistance appears more closely linked to failure of effective antigen presentation, T-cell exclusion or dysfunction, and broader remodeling of the Hodgkin lymphoma microenvironment despite persistent 9p24.1-driven immune susceptibility [4,5]. These differences provide the rationale for non-cross-resistant sequencing and for combining checkpoint blockade with cytotoxic or CD30-directed therapy.

An important clinical observation is that prior PD-1 blockade may sensitize patients to subsequent therapies, including allogeneic transplantation, but it also raises concern for immune-mediated toxicity, necessitating careful interval planning and graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis [2,6]. Overall, sequencing is therefore less algorithmic than risk-adapted: remission depth, prior exposure, transplant intent, and mechanism-based resistance should guide selection of the next therapy.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Biomarkers for prognosis and treatment selection
subsections.content:
Biomarker development in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is increasingly oriented toward integrating tumor genetics, the immune microenvironment, and functional imaging to refine risk stratification beyond conventional stage- and bulk-based models. Baseline metabolic tumor volume on FDG-PET has emerged as a reproducible adverse marker associated with inferior progression-free survival, particularly when interpreted alongside early treatment response, supporting a move toward composite biologic-risk frameworks rather than reliance on anatomy alone ref [155].

Among tissue biomarkers, recurrent 9p24.1 copy-number gains or amplifications drive PD-L1/PD-L2 expression and represent one of the clearest biologic predictors of sensitivity to PD-1 blockade in relapsed/refractory disease, providing a mechanistic rationale for biomarker-informed use of checkpoint inhibitors ref [23]. Epstein-Barr virus status may also define biologically distinct subsets through effects on Reed-Sternberg cell signaling and immune composition, although its prognostic value remains context dependent and not yet treatment-directing in routine practice ref [156].

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a particularly promising translational biomarker because it enables noninvasive genotyping and dynamic disease assessment despite the scarcity of malignant cells in cHL biopsies. Sequencing studies have shown that plasma genotyping can capture recurrent alterations, including lesions affecting JAK-STAT and immune evasion pathways, and may complement tissue analyses for both prognosis and therapeutic selection ref [157], ref [158]. The near-term challenge is prospective validation: biomarkers must demonstrate added value over interim PET and establish actionable thresholds that can guide de-escalation, intensification, or selection of targeted combinations in clinically heterogeneous patient populations ref [155], ref [158].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
The contemporary therapeutic landscape in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is increasingly defined by rational combinations that exploit the disease’s unique biology, particularly CD30 expression and pervasive PD-1/PD-L1 axis activation. Antibody-drug conjugates and immune checkpoint inhibitors have each shown substantial single-agent activity in relapsed disease, creating a foundation for chemo-sparing or response-adapted regimens across treatment lines. Brentuximab vedotin improved outcomes when incorporated into frontline therapy with A+AVD in advanced-stage disease, establishing proof that targeted agents can outperform legacy cytotoxic backbones in selected settings ref [15]. Likewise, nivolumab and pembrolizumab have demonstrated high response rates in heavily pretreated cHL, validating immune evasion as a therapeutically actionable hallmark ref [20], ref [142].

Current combinatorial strategies aim to deepen remission while limiting cumulative toxicity. Dual or sequential integration of brentuximab vedotin with PD-1 blockade is especially attractive because it couples direct tumor targeting with reinvigoration of antitumor immunity; early-phase data for nivolumab plus brentuximab vedotin in relapsed/refractory cHL showed high complete response rates and manageable safety, supporting its use as a bridge to transplantation or, potentially, as part of non-transplant pathways ref [159]. In the frontline setting, checkpoint blockade-containing regimens such as nivolumab-AVD have also produced compelling efficacy and tolerability, suggesting that immunochemotherapy may further reduce relapse risk without escalating late effects associated with more intensive approaches ref [160].

Future work should clarify optimal sequencing, duration, and patient selection for these agents, particularly whether biologically informed combinations can replace conventional chemotherapy in subsets with favorable immune sensitivity. Priorities include integrating novel small molecules, refining transplantation-sparing strategies, and balancing efficacy against neuropathy, immune-related toxicity, infertility risk, and survivorship burden.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Minimal residual disease and disease monitoring
subsections.content:
In classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), disease monitoring has historically relied on fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT, particularly interim PET after two cycles, because imaging captures treatment responsiveness even when the malignant Hodgkin Reed–Sternberg population is sparse. The prognostic value of response-adapted PET was established in advanced-stage disease and now underpins both de-escalation and escalation strategies, but PET remains an indirect surrogate of tumor burden and is limited by false-positive inflammatory uptake and imperfect specificity for persistent viable disease [1,2].

These limitations have intensified interest in molecular minimal residual disease (MRD) assays. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is especially attractive in cHL because recurrent somatic alterations, including 9p24.1 copy-number changes and other lymphoma-associated lesions, can be tracked in plasma despite low tumor cellularity in tissue biopsies. Early studies showed that plasma genotyping can recover the genomic landscape of cHL and that ctDNA dynamics during therapy correlate with metabolic response and outcome, supporting a complementary role alongside PET rather than simple replacement [3,4].

The next challenge is standardization and clinical qualification. Prospective work is needed to define assay sensitivity thresholds, optimal sampling time points, and how to act on discordant PET/ctDNA results, particularly in patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors where inflammatory flare may confound imaging. Integrating molecular monitoring with imaging and clinical risk factors could ultimately refine end-of-treatment assessment, identify impending relapse earlier, and provide a more biologically grounded platform for adaptive trials in cHL [4,5].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Long-term survivorship and quality of life
subsections.content:
Because contemporary therapy cures most patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), survivorship has become a central endpoint alongside disease control. Long-term follow-up studies consistently show excess late mortality from second malignant neoplasms and cardiovascular disease, particularly after historical large-field radiotherapy and alkylator- or anthracycline-containing regimens, underscoring the need to embed risk-adapted survivorship planning into frontline decision-making rather than treating it as a post hoc concern ref [166], ref [110]. These observations provide a major rationale for modern efforts to reduce radiation exposure, limit cumulative chemotherapy toxicity, and individualize treatment intensity.

Quality of life after cHL is multidimensional and extends beyond relapse-free survival. Survivors may experience persistent fatigue, neuropathy, impaired physical functioning, psychosocial distress, sexual dysfunction, and infertility concerns; these burdens can remain substantial even in younger adults who are otherwise cured. The GHSG analyses highlight that patient-reported outcomes differ meaningfully by treatment intensity and trajectory over time, supporting incorporation of PROs into comparative trials and survivorship clinics ref [167]. In parallel, anthracycline exposure and mediastinal irradiation continue to shape late cardiovascular risk, while chest irradiation and some systemic regimens contribute to excess risks of breast, lung, and other second cancers, necessitating tailored screening and prevention strategies ref [168], ref [169].

Future survivorship care in cHL should therefore integrate longitudinal risk stratification, fertility preservation, cardiovascular prevention, vaccination and infection counseling, mental health support, and structured survivorship surveillance. Importantly, newer regimens that omit bleomycin or reduce radiotherapy may improve some late outcomes, but the survivorship consequences of checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates remain incompletely defined, making long-duration follow-up essential in both clinical trials and real-world cohorts ref [170].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
De-escalation versus intensification has become a central organizing principle in contemporary cHL management, reflecting the need to preserve excellent cure rates while reducing late toxicity. The strongest evidence for response-adapted de-escalation comes from interim PET-guided strategies. In advanced-stage disease, the RATHL trial showed that omission of bleomycin after a negative interim PET could reduce pulmonary toxicity without materially compromising efficacy, supporting treatment attenuation in early responders ref [14]. In early-stage disease, the RAPID and H10 studies demonstrated both the promise and the limits of PET-adapted omission of radiotherapy: reduced treatment burden is feasible for selected patients, but often at the cost of a modest increase in relapse risk that must be weighed against long-term toxicity concerns ref [171], ref [109].

Conversely, intensification remains appropriate for biologically or clinically high-risk disease and for patients with inadequate early response. Escalated BEACOPP improved tumor control compared with ABVD in randomized trials, but this benefit must be balanced against infertility, myelosuppression, infection risk, and secondary malignancies, limiting broad adoption as a universal strategy ref [13]. This tension has shifted the field toward selective intensification rather than routine escalation, using early metabolic response, baseline risk factors, and increasingly molecular markers to identify the minority most likely to benefit from more aggressive therapy.

The emerging challenge is therefore not choosing de-escalation or intensification in the abstract, but matching each paradigm to patient-specific relapse risk and survivorship priorities. Modern regimens incorporating brentuximab vedotin or checkpoint blockade may further reframe this trade-off by enabling chemotherapy reduction without sacrificing disease control, although mature comparative and long-term safety data are still needed ref [15]. Future trial design will likely emphasize integrated risk models that combine PET, circulating tumor DNA, and patient-reported outcomes to individualize both treatment burden and curative intent.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Unmet needs in special and underrepresented populations
subsections.content:
Important evidence gaps in classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) persist for populations that are systematically underrepresented in trials, including older adults, people living with HIV, pregnant patients, and those treated in low-resource settings. Older patients have inferior outcomes that reflect both adverse biology and treatment intolerance; registry and cooperative-group analyses show higher treatment-related mortality and lower progression-free survival with standard anthracycline- and bleomycin-containing approaches, underscoring the need for geriatric assessment, toxicity-sparing regimens, and endpoints beyond cure alone ref [116], ref [172].

People living with HIV now achieve substantially better results in the antiretroviral era, but they remain excluded from many prospective studies despite distinct interactions among immune dysregulation, Epstein-Barr virus biology, comorbidity, and supportive-care needs. Contemporary reviews emphasize that modern cHL therapy can be delivered effectively in this group, yet prospective data for checkpoint inhibitors, brentuximab vedotin-containing combinations, and response-adapted strategies remain sparse ref [173]. Pregnancy-associated cHL is another area where evidence is driven largely by retrospective series; available data support individualized balancing of maternal disease control and fetal safety, but there is little high-level evidence to guide imaging, timing of therapy, and postpartum management ref [174].

Geographic inequity is an equally important unmet need. In low- and middle-income countries, delayed diagnosis, limited PET access, constrained pathology infrastructure, and restricted availability of novel agents may widen survival disparities and hinder implementation of biomarker-guided care. Global oncology analyses argue that future trial design should deliberately include older adults, HIV-associated cHL, adolescents and young adults outside pediatric/medical oncology silos, and resource-stratified cohorts, while embedding patient-reported outcomes, fertility, and survivorship endpoints to ensure that therapeutic advances are generalizable ref [175].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Precision Oncology, Survivorship, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Future research priorities and trial design
subsections.content:
Future cHL trials should move beyond one-size-fits-all escalation/de-escalation and instead prospectively integrate baseline biology, early treatment response, and patient-centered endpoints. The feasibility of PET-adapted designs has already been established in large randomized studies, but next-generation protocols should combine metabolic response with circulating tumor DNA, host factors, and treatment-related vulnerability to define biologically coherent risk groups rather than relying on stage alone ref [95], ref [176]. Such platforms are particularly important as highly active agents permit multiple curative pathways with different late-toxicity profiles.

Methodologically, priority should be given to adaptive, biomarker-stratified, and seamlessly randomized platform trials that can evaluate chemotherapy minimization, antibody-drug conjugates, checkpoint blockade, and radiotherapy omission within the same master protocol. Endpoints also require modernization: progression-free survival remains important, but durable remission off treatment, fertility preservation, cardiopulmonary outcomes, second malignancies, and patient-reported quality of life should be embedded as co-primary or key secondary outcomes, consistent with survivorship data from long-term cohorts ref [177]. International harmonization of response assessment and correlative sampling, including standardized PET interpretation and molecular residual disease assays, will be essential for cross-trial comparability ref [80].

Finally, trial design must address persistent evidence gaps by deliberately enrolling older adults, children transitioning to adult care, pregnant patients when feasible, and racially and geographically underrepresented populations. Contemporary studies in older or frail patients illustrate both the necessity and feasibility of tailored eligibility criteria and toxicity-aware regimens ref [178]. Cooperative-group and registry-linked pragmatic trials may therefore be crucial to generate externally valid evidence for populations historically excluded from pivotal studies.
